acumatica.name: Acumatica
acumatica.tagline: Acumatica Cloud ERP, wired into Craft Commerce.
acumatica.lede: Products, stock, customers and credit in; orders out — through the contract-based REST endpoint.
acumatica.connect: A dedicated integration user, the endpoint version from Web Service Endpoints, and optionally the branch and warehouse orders are raised against.

traps.title: One session per run, not per request
traps.body: It signs in once, shares both session cookies across the run and signs out after — so a small licence is not spent on logins.

traps.title: Every value is unwrapped
traps.body: Contract payloads send {"value": …} for every field. The connector unwraps them before anything reaches Commerce.

traps.title: Stock you can actually sell
traps.body: Read from the inventory summary inquiry, per warehouse, with allocations taken off — not the company-wide shelf figure.

mapping.lede: Endpoints get extended. When your web SKU lives in a custom field, one rule on the mapping screen points the connector at it — no fork, no waiting for a release.

rules.note: A canonical target overrides what the connector read. Note the .value — the raw payload is still wrapped.

afas.name: AFAS
afas.lede: Items, prices, stock, debtors and credit in; sales orders out — through your own GetConnectors and UpdateConnectors.
afas.connect: AFAS has no fixed schema — your partner built the GetConnectors. So every connector name, the modified-date field and the item and customer keys are settings.

traps.title: The token, wrapped twice
traps.body: Paste the part between <data> tags. Erpy wraps it and base64-encodes it into AfasToken, which is the step that usually earns a 401.

traps.title: Three filter lists kept in step
traps.body: AFAS takes field ids, values and operators as parallel lists. One out of step filters on the wrong field and quietly returns the wrong rows.

traps.title: Prices from whichever column exists
traps.body: Prijs, Price or Verkoopprijs, in that order — and anything else is one mapping rule away.

mapping.lede: AFAS is the ERP the mapping overlay was built for. Whatever your partner called a column, a canonical rule points the connector at it before anything reaches Commerce.

rules.note: Overrides the price the connector read from your prices GetConnector.

businesscentral.name: Business Central
businesscentral.tagline: Dynamics 365 Business Central, wired into Craft Commerce.
businesscentral.lede: Items, prices, stock, customers, invoices and credit in; sales orders out — through API v2.0 and an Entra ID app.
businesscentral.connect: An Entra ID app registration with client credentials — no consent screen, because nobody is awake for a nightly stock sync — plus the environment and company.

traps.title: Prices the standard API never had
traps.body: Point it at a sales-prices page you publish as an API, and at a posted-shipments page for tracking numbers. Leave either blank and the run log says why.

traps.title: blocked is not a yes/no
traps.body: Blank, Ship, Invoice or All. Any of the three stops brings the customer through on hold.

traps.title: Throttling, honoured
traps.body: Business Central answers 429 with a Retry-After it means. The transport waits that long instead of hammering the environment.

mapping.lede: A published page is yours, so its field names are whatever your developer chose. Correct the connector on the mapping screen instead of republishing the page.

rules.note: Your sales-prices page calls it salesPrice; the connector expected unitPrice.

exactonline.name: Exact Online
exactonline.lede: Items, prices, stock, accounts, invoices and credit in; sales orders out — through Exact’s REST API, per division.
exactonline.connect: Your own app registration for your region, then the division. A wrong division answers with an empty, entirely successful response — so the test checks for it.

traps.title: Refresh tokens that rotate
traps.body: Every refresh spends the old token. Erpy writes the new one back straight away, so the connection survives the second refresh.

traps.title: A daily rate limit
traps.body: About one call a second and a hard cap per day. The transport stays under the minute limit and honours Retry-After for the rest.

traps.title: Dates as /Date(ms)/
traps.body: OData v2 dates arrive as wrapped epoch milliseconds, which no date parser reads. The connector converts them.

mapping.lede: The connector reads the item’s Code. If your shop sells under another item field, one rule points it there — no fork, no waiting for a release.

rules.note: A canonical target overrides what the connector read, before it reaches Commerce.

myob.name: MYOB
myob.tagline: MYOB Acumatica and MYOB Exo, wired into Craft Commerce.
myob.lede: Two connectors in one add-on: MYOB Acumatica (formerly Advanced) through its REST API, and Exo through the Exo API gateway.
myob.connect: Exo wants a developer key, an Exo user and — hosted — a MYOB account login, and gives the same 401 when any one is wrong. So each is its own labelled field.

traps.title: The Exo token is not the Basic header
traps.body: The Exo user goes in x-myobapi-exotoken, the MYOB account in Authorization. Swap them and correct credentials still fail.

traps.title: Two levels of stop
traps.body: stopcredit 1 warns and 2 blocks. Both arrive on hold, because either means nobody should sell on account without looking.

traps.title: One session on Acumatica
traps.body: MYOB counts concurrent sessions against your licence, so the connector signs in once per run and signs out afterwards.

mapping.lede: Exo reads a product’s price from sellprice1. If your web price is another band, one rule on the mapping screen corrects it.

rules.note: On MYOB Acumatica the same rule unwraps the value: raw.DefaultPrice.value.

netsuite.name: NetSuite
netsuite.lede: Items, prices, stock, customers, invoices and credit in; sales orders out — SuiteTalk REST with every bulk read in SuiteQL.
netsuite.connect: Token-Based Authentication: an integration record and an access token, plus the subsidiary and location orders are raised against.

traps.title: Bulk reads in SuiteQL
traps.body: The record API returns links, one fetch per item. SuiteQL returns whole rows a thousand at a time — the difference between minutes and all night.

traps.title: externalId as the key
traps.body: NetSuite refuses a second order with the same external id, so even two racing workers cannot book one sale twice.

traps.title: One account id, three spellings
traps.body: Enter it as NetSuite shows it. The host, the OAuth realm and the signature each get the form they want from that one setting.

mapping.lede: The connector reads the SKU from itemid. If you sell under the UPC, one rule points it there — no fork, no waiting for a release.

rules.note: A canonical target overrides what the connector read, before it reaches Commerce.

odoo.name: Odoo
odoo.lede: Products, pricelists, stock, partners, invoices and credit in; quotations out — Community or Enterprise, over JSON-RPC.
odoo.connect: Your Odoo URL, the database, and a login with an API key rather than a password — plus the warehouse and sales team orders belong to.

traps.title: Errors that arrive as HTTP 200
traps.body: A missing model, a permission failure and a traceback all come back as success. The connector reads the body, so the log shows the real error.

traps.title: Relations as [id, "Name"]
traps.body: Many-to-one fields are two-element arrays. The connector unpacks them; on the mapping screen, raw.categ_id.1 is the name.

traps.title: UTC with no marker
traps.body: write_date is UTC and doesn’t say so. The watermark is converted first, so a site west of Greenwich doesn’t skip hours of changes.

mapping.lede: If your catalogue keys on the barcode rather than the Internal Reference, one rule on the mapping screen corrects the SKU.

rules.note: Odoo sends an empty field as false; nullif: skips it, so a product with no barcode keeps its reference.

priority.name: Priority
priority.lede: Parts, stock, customers, invoices and credit in; orders out — through OData, addressing the same forms your consultant uses.
priority.connect: Priority exposes its forms — LOGPART, CUSTOMERS, ORDERS — and every installation customises them. So every form name is a setting.

traps.title: OBLIGO is the credit limit
traps.body: The word means “liability” and catches everybody reading the schema for the first time. Credit reads it, with the balance and the block flag.

traps.title: Archived parts stay archived
traps.body: Priority archives rather than deletes. A part with PARTARC set arrives blocked and never reaches the storefront.

traps.title: Header and lines in one request
traps.body: The order and its lines sub-form go together, so a refused line never leaves an orphaned header behind.

mapping.lede: Because every Priority is customised, this is the screen you will come back to. A canonical rule points the connector at your column — no fork, no release.

rules.note: Your implementation keeps the web part number in a custom column.

sage.name: Sage
sage.tagline: Sage Intacct, 200, X3 and Accounting, wired into Craft Commerce.
sage.lede: Sage sells four unrelated products under one name. One add-on, four connectors — pick the one you run.
sage.connect: Intacct wants a sender id issued to the integration and a Web Services user in the company — and the sender authorised under Web Services Authorizations.

traps.title: Intacct pages by resultId
traps.body: Not by offset. The connector follows the result id Intacct hands back, so large reads neither repeat nor skip.

traps.title: Sage 200 needs X-Site
traps.body: A bearer token, the subscription key and the site header on every request. Without the site, an authenticated request quietly returns nothing.

traps.title: Accounting is not an ERP
traps.body: No sales orders, no warehouses. So it doesn’t pretend: a completed order is posted as a sales invoice, which is what merchants ask for.

mapping.lede: Whichever Sage you run, a canonical rule points the connector at the field you actually sell under — no fork, no waiting for a release.

rules.note: On X3 the same rule reads raw.EANCOD.

sapb1.name: SAP Business One
sapb1.tagline: SAP Business One, wired into Craft Commerce.
sapb1.lede: Items, price lists, stock, business partners, invoices and credit in; sales orders out — through the Service Layer.
sapb1.connect: The Service Layer URL, the company database and a B1 user of its own — every login takes a licence slot, so Erpy shares one session per run.

traps.title: tNO is not true
traps.body: B1 answers booleans as strings, and (bool) 'tNO' is true in PHP. That is how integrations publish every frozen item. Not this one.

traps.title: Both cookies, every time
traps.body: On a load-balanced Service Layer the session lives on one node, and ROUTEID is what gets back to it. The connector sends both.

traps.title: 20 rows, unless asked
traps.body: The Service Layer ignores $top without an explicit page-size preference. The connector sets it.

mapping.lede: The connector reads the SKU from ItemCode. If you sell under the barcode, or a user-defined field, one rule points it there.

rules.note: B1 prefixes user-defined fields U_, and they are all in the raw payload.

unit4.name: Unit4
unit4.tagline: Unit4 ERPx and Business World, wired into Craft Commerce.
unit4.lede: Products, stock, customers and credit in; sales orders out — with every resource path a setting, because no two estates match.
unit4.connect: Which resources exist depends on your modules and your partner. Every path is a setting, the defaults are ERPx’s, and both authentication schemes are offered.

traps.title: Collections wrapped four ways
traps.body: data, items, value, results — or bare. It depends on the resource and the release. The connector tries each.

traps.title: Field names that vary
traps.body: The SKU from productId, id or code; stock from quantity or balance. It reads the first that exists.

traps.title: Mandatory fields your estate added
traps.body: Anything you put in an order’s customFields is sent with it — the way to fill a project or cost-centre code.

mapping.lede: On Unit4 this isn’t an edge case, it’s part of setting up. A canonical rule points the connector at your estate’s field names.

rules.note: Your products resource calls the item code articleCode.

visma.name: Visma
visma.lede: Inventory, stock, customers, invoices and credit in; sales orders out — through the integration API and Visma Connect.
visma.connect: A Visma Connect client, the scope, and the company id — a wrong company answers with a successful empty list, so the connection test checks for it.

traps.title: Delta needs two parameters
traps.body: Send lastModifiedDateTime without its condition and Visma returns everything — a delta sync that works until somebody times it.

traps.title: One company, every request
traps.body: Everything is scoped by the ipp-company-id header. The connector sends it on every call, and the test catches it missing.

traps.title: Look-ups that change shape
traps.body: Some values arrive as {value, description}, the same field elsewhere as a bare string. The connector accepts both.

mapping.lede: The connector reads the SKU from inventoryNumber. If your web SKU lives elsewhere, one rule on the mapping screen points it there.

rules.note: Where a field is a look-up, add .value and check the preview.
